column3: Its formula "truth of certainty" directly reinforces the focus's emphatic truth claim.
God's unchangeable word and denial of injustice ground the announced outcome as settled and just.
Links truth from the Lord to a prepared enclosing Fire, though it does not depict the dispute.
Divine will, reverence, and forgiveness add only a distant counterpoint to the Fire scene.
The oath by the Quran supplies local revelation context but no added account of the Fire's dispute.
Names God as the true authority and best final outcome, supporting the focus's reality claim indirectly.
States that the Lord's word became due upon disbelievers: they are the companions of the Fire.
Immediately introduces a band entering with the addressees and already roasting in the Fire.
Humanity's emergence as an open disputant supplies a broad antecedent to the later quarrel.
The demand for a heavenly book and Israel's earlier transgression do not clarify the Fire's dispute.
The promise of multiplied reward does not clarify the truth claim or the dispute in Hell.
Joseph's instruction concerning his father and family has no useful connection to the focus.
The fueled Fire is only a lexical image, without its inhabitants or their contention.
Its local doubt and not-yet-tasted punishment contextualize the certainty later asserted in the surah.
God declares both the truth and truthful speech, closely anchoring the focus's emphatic assertion.
Answers whether the threatened event is true: it is true and cannot be escaped.
The entrants blame those who brought this fate upon them, directly advancing the Hell dispute.
Mockers returning merrily to their households does not add to the final dispute.
Its oath that the promise is true strengthens certainty, but lacks the Fire and quarrel setting.
A settled morning punishment provides a broad consequence, not the focus's afterlife contention.
Explicitly says the idolaters will be disputing therein, supplying the closest direct parallel.
Names disbelievers as abiding in Hell, adding the inhabitants but not their dispute.
The command to remember David does not illuminate the Fire scene.
The fixed pattern of evil recoil offers only a general justice framework for the announced outcome.
Abraham's rescue from a worldly fire is a contrast, not an account of the people of Hell.
The disputants ask for doubled Fire punishment for whoever brought it to them, continuing the scene.
The upper assembly's dispute distinguishes another kind of contention from the people of Fire's quarrel.
Identifies Fire as the enduring recompense for enemies who denied God's signs.
The gathered deniers of signs supply judgment context but no Fire or dispute.
The delayed coming of clear proof to disbelievers is only remote background to their final condition.
Judging between people by truth uses dispute language in a legal, not eschatological, setting.
The disputants seeking judgment by truth form a local contrast to the irreparable dispute in Hell.
The instruction to ask those with knowledge does not add to the focus.
Dishonest conduct by some People of the Book is unrelated to the Fire's dispute.
The divine question exposes denial without knowledge, providing only general accountability context.
The announcement of the litigants' story gives local lexical context but no link to Hell.
Envy after truth became clear is distant from the final dispute and Fire scene.
Reflection on the revealed book supports reception of the warning only generally.
The evil assumption about believers returning home does not clarify the focus.
A dispute over Mary's guardianship is unrelated to the people of Fire.
God forbids disputing before Him because warning had already been given, directly explaining its futility.
Contrasts believers who know the Hour is true with those who dispute it, supporting the focus's certainty.
Its final designation of apostates as companions of Fire adds little after clearer Fire passages.
Job's restored family is unrelated to the announced Fire dispute.
Calls the opponents a contentious people and describes their argument as mere disputation.
Two parties dispute about their Lord, and the disbelieving side receives garments of Fire.
The written book alone does not add to the focus.
Lot's prayer for rescue from his people's deeds is not about the people of Fire disputing.
Repeats the formula "truth of certainty," confirming the focus's first assertion after 69:51.
The remembrance of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob does not clarify the focus.
The coming destruction of an unjust town gives only a broad judgment parallel.
The Fire punishment for disbelievers restates an outcome already more fully established.
The word falls upon wrongdoers and silences them, a useful contrast to the Fire's active quarrel.
Describes someone intensely contentious, supplying a general human pattern but no eschatological setting.
Their return to Hell is a bare destination statement with no further explanation.
The list of exemplary servants is unrelated to the Fire dispute.
Thamud's response to Salih divides them into two groups disputing, a worldly antecedent to contention.
The criminals' abiding torment in Hell adds little beyond earlier direct Fire descriptions.
Denial and following desires provide general moral background to a settled outcome.
Truth from the Lord and the prohibition on doubt reinforce the focus's assertion of reality.
The people of al-Aykah being wrongdoers does not clarify the Fire's dispute.
The good final return for the God-conscious is a contrast without added detail on the focus.
All parties will dispute before their Lord on Resurrection Day, directly framing final accountable contention.
The declaration of great success is unrelated to the people of Fire.
Declares the Lord's punishment inevitable, reinforcing the certainty of the Fire scene.
The parable of truth enduring and falsehood vanishing offers only a general truth framework.
Patience and forgiveness concern earthly conflict, not the final quarrel.
The promised Day of Account in the local surah does not itself clarify the dispute.
Warns believers to guard themselves and families from Fire, but adds no account of its inhabitants' contention.
Its general lesson for one who fears adds little to the specific Fire scene.
The call for people to assemble is unrelated to the focus.
The messenger's warning mission and lack of liability for Hell's people supply responsibility context.
The word of punishment becoming due and the inability to rescue one in Fire support the settled outcome.
Adam's formation and the angels' prostration do not clarify the focus.
Temporal provision followed by compulsion to Fire gives a general final-destination parallel.
The blessing upon Abraham's household is unrelated to the focus.
The messenger conveys while God reckons, offering only broad judgment context.
Moses's request for a minister from his family is unrelated to the focus.
A general sign for believers does not add to the Fire dispute.
The known appointed time alone does not clarify the people of Fire's contention.
Its statement about inability to articulate in dispute is a remote lexical parallel only.
Disagreement over the book in deep schism is a broad contrast to the final dispute.
The Quran as a reminder to all worlds supplies local context but no added account of the focus.
Rejecting confirming truth supplies a general cause of judgment, not the Fire's contention.
God's comprehensive knowledge and record do not clarify the focus.
Future belief and testimony concerning People of the Book provide only distant judgment context.
Identifies God as the true Lord and contrasts truth with error, supporting the first clause generally.
Names the Fire as the appointed place for a rejecting party while affirming revealed truth.
The townspeople's complacency before punishment does not add to the focus's final dispute.
Lot and his family being saved is unrelated to the people of Fire.
The companions of Paradise enjoying themselves provide no useful detail on the focus.
Contrasts empty human speech with God's true speech, a distant support for the truth assertion.
A blazing Fire is a bare image already covered by stronger Fire passages.
Truth's arrival and falsehood's collapse offer a general truth contrast without the final scene.
Pharaoh's accusation of sorcery does not clarify the people of Fire disputing.
Truth does not follow human desires, giving a broad account of truth's independent standard.
Opposing God and His messenger leads to abiding Hell, a redundant consequence statement.
Moses's commitment to speak only truth provides a distant verbal parallel to the focus's truth claim.
The forgetful idolater is said to be among the companions of Fire, adding only a generic cause.
The truthful Moses-Pharaoh account offers a general narrative use of truth, not the Fire dispute.
Immediately sets the transgressors' evil final return before the people of Fire are shown speaking.
Names Hell as the wretched resting place in the focus's immediate local setting.
Its boiling-water punishment supplies sensory context but not the quarrel itself.
The other matching punishments extend the local scene without explaining the dispute.
The Fire's people ask why absent men they counted wicked are not seen, continuing their exchange.
Their uncertainty over former ridicule immediately precedes and clarifies the summary of their dispute.
Each nation entering the Fire curses its sister nation, directly depicting hostile relations among its people.
The later nation tells the earlier that neither has favor and demands shared punishment.
The people of Fire call to the people of Paradise for water, expanding the scene's failed speech.
Followed leaders disown their followers when they see punishment and all ties are severed.
Followers blame those they followed after seeing the Fire, extending the reciprocal rupture.
Humans and jinn answer God concerning their mutual exploitation before their Fire abode is named.
The warning to humans and jinn provides the prior accountability framework for that final exchange.
On the Day of gathering, idolaters are separated from their alleged partners.
God's testimony ends the false worshipers' claimed relation to their partners.
Each soul learns what it sent ahead and false claims abandon their makers.
Followers and leaders argue before God, with leaders denying power to rescue their followers.
Alleged partners repudiate idolaters and call their claims lies on the final day.
God questions the objects of worship about whether they led His servants astray.
Those objects deny the charge and state that the people themselves forgot the reminder.
God's summons asking for alleged partners stages the final exposure of false allegiance.
The leaders admit they led others astray and formally disavow those who worshiped them.
The repeated question about alleged partners reinforces the judgment setting of repudiated claims.
In the Fire, the condemned say they obeyed their masters and great ones instead of God.
They assign the blame for their misguidance to those leaders.
They ask that those leaders receive doubled punishment and a great curse.
Wrongdoers exchange blame before their Lord as the weak accuse the arrogant of blocking faith.
The arrogant deny coercion and return responsibility to the weak.
Both groups conceal remorse as punishment appears, completing the mutual-blame scene.
The condemned turn toward one another and question each other before their shared punishment.
Followers accuse the others of having approached them with deceptive authority.
The accused answer that the followers themselves were not believers.
They deny having authority over them and identify them as transgressors.
They acknowledge that their Lord's word has become due upon them all.
The misleaders admit leading others astray because they were astray themselves.
It concludes that all parties share the punishment that Day.
The speakers confess before God that they were in manifest error.
They identify the error as equating false objects of worship with the Lord of the worlds.
They blame the criminals for leading them astray, developing the dispute's accusation.
Their lack of intercessors shows the failure of the alliances invoked in the Fire dialogue.
Their lack of a devoted friend completes the collapse of solidarity behind the contention.
Those driven to Hell answer its keepers that warners had indeed come to them.
The keepers command entry into Hell as the outcome of that acknowledged warning.
The weak and arrogant explicitly dispute with one another in the Fire over their shared fate.
The arrogant answer that all are in the Fire and God has judged between servants.
The people of Fire ask Hell's keepers to seek even one day's easing of punishment.
The keepers answer by recalling the rejected clear signs and deny relief to the disbelievers.
Disbelievers in the Fire ask to see the jinn and humans who misled them so they may be abased.
The people of Hell call to Malik to end them, and he answers that they will remain.
The reply attributes their condition to their aversion to the truth brought to them.
Hell's keepers ask its incoming people whether a warner came to them.
They admit the warner came but confess that they denied him.
They acknowledge that hearing or reasoning would have kept them from the blazing Fire.
Their confession of sin identifies them as the companions of the Blaze.
The companions of the right ask about the criminals, introducing an afterlife accounting dialogue.
The criminals answer the question of what brought them into Saqar.
They identify neglect of prayer as one element of that answer.
They identify failure to feed the poor as another element of the answer.
They admit joining those who engaged in vain discourse.
They admit denying the Day of Recompense until certainty came.
Its arrival of certainty completes the criminals' explanation of their Fire outcome.
